beats.narration_text: Merhaba. This is Liam, in for Bear. write_review_queue_report.py is the last step in the Brutalist audit chain — the moment two JSON files become a human-readable markdown report. It reads machine data from audit.json and your visual findings from review-notes.json, and writes AUDIT.md without touching a single reel.

beats.narration_text: write_review_queue_report.py doesn't audit anything. It takes two JSON files — audit.json with machine-measured data and review-notes.json with your visual findings — and turns them into a readable markdown report. The actual auditing happened earlier. This script is the pen that writes the summary. Read-only by design: the docstring says it plain — never mutate reels.

beats.narration_text: The script takes two files in, writes one file out. audit.json carries machine-measured data — reel hashes, durations, slate counts, stale status. review-notes.json carries your human visual findings — what you saw on screen, ranked by priority. write_review_queue_report.py combines them into AUDIT.md, one section per reel. The reels themselves are never touched.

beats.narration_text: Line one: the output directory is the only argument. The script reads audit.json from that folder and expects an exact schema — reels as a list of rows, each row carrying reel number, reel path, probe data, and stale status. review-notes.json maps reel numbers to priority and finding strings. Miss either file or misname a key and the script crashes. There is no try-except.

props.title: write_review_queue_report.py — reading inputs
props.code:
out   = Path(sys.argv[1])
audit = json.loads((out / 'audit.json').read_text())
notes = json.loads((out / 'review-notes.json').read_text())
rows  = audit['reels']

# audit.json schema: { "reels": [{"number": 1, "reel": "...",
#   "width": 3840, "height": 2160, "duration": "224.5",
#   "stale": false, "declared_slates": [] }] }

# review-notes.json schema: { "1": {"priority": "LOW",
#   "finding": "your visual findings..." } }

beats.narration_text: For each reel, the script looks up the human note by number — stored in review-notes.json as a string key. The priority and finding go into a bold markdown header. Below that: the master probe data — width, height, duration, stale flag, declared slate count. Then it reads the reel's beat_sheet.json and scans every beat for pantry references.

show.event: note = notes[str(n)] reveals — terracotta accent on str(n)

props.title: write_review_queue_report.py — main loop
props.code:
for row in rows:
    n    = row['number']
    note = notes[str(n)]      # str key lookup — KeyError if missing
    reel = Path(row['reel'])
    text += [
        f'### {n:02d}. {reel.name}', '',
        f'**{note["priority"]}** — {note["finding"]}', '',
        f'Master probe: {row["width"]} × {row["height"]}; '
        f'{float(row["duration"] or 0):.1f}s; '
        f'stale at snapshot: {row["stale"]}; ...',
    ]
    sheet = json.loads((reel / 'beat_sheet.json').read_text())

beats.narration_text: The script flags every beat that still has a pantry reference — an image slot waiting on a human to source it. The comment in the code names it plainly: all three legacy spellings occur in this queue — pantry_path, pantry_file, and pantry. This is backward compatibility written as a comment, not hidden in a migration script. The schema evolved; the reader handles all three forms.

show.event: Comment reveals: # All three legacy spellings occur in this queue.

props.title: write_review_queue_report.py — pantry flags
props.code:
for beat in sheet.get('beats', []):
        shot   = beat.get('shot') or {}
        # All three legacy spellings occur in this queue.
        path = (shot.get('pantry_path') or
                shot.get('pantry_file') or
                shot.get('pantry'))
        if path:
            intent = (shot.get('visual_intent') or
                      shot.get('brief') or
                      shot.get('subject') or '')
            text += [f'- **{beat["beat_id"]}** — {intent}']

beats.narration_text: AUDIT.md has a fixed structure: a scope statement, main findings, rules and tooling changes, repair order, a section for every film — priority, finding, master probe, reel link, and any pantry-requesting beats. That structure is baked into Python string literals. The script author decided which sections matter. You cannot configure it — if the report shape needs to change, change the source.

show.event: Sections reveal one by one: Scope → Main findings
Per-film section expands: probe + pantry flags

props.heading: Hardcoded report sections
props.body: Scope statement · Main findings · Rules and tooling changed · Repair order · Per-film section (priority, finding, master probe, reel link, pantry flags) · Audit artifacts and limits. All section text is Python string literals in the script — not a template, not configurable. The shape of the report is a design decision baked into the source.
props.quote: "Do not change human approvals or publish in response to this audit. Changing skills does not retroactively repair an MP4."
props.verdictLabel: Report structure is a design decision, not a parameter.

beats.narration_text: The script has no error handling. That is intentional. If audit.json is missing you get a FileNotFoundError. If a reel number is in audit.json but not in review-notes.json you get a KeyError. If a reel folder moved since audit_review_queue.py ran, the beat_sheet.json read crashes. These failures tell you exactly what to fix. A silent pass on bad inputs would be worse.

show.event: IndexError: list index out of range (no argument)

props.title: write_review_queue_report.py — failure modes
props.code:
# No try-except. Crash is the contract.

# 1. No argument given:
#    IndexError: list index out of range
#    Fix: python3 write_review_queue_report.py <out-dir>

# 2. Missing audit.json in out-dir:
#    FileNotFoundError: .../audit.json
#    Fix: run audit_review_queue.py first

# 3. Reel number not in review-notes.json:
#    KeyError: '1'
#    Fix: add matching entry to review-notes.json

# 4. Reel folder moved since audit ran:
#    FileNotFoundError: .../beat_sheet.json
props.sparkLine: Each crash names what is missing.

beats.narration_text: The report is honest about its own limits. Twelve frames per film at 70% position is a heuristic — it catches settled-state defects but misses mid-animation states. Pantry flags are metadata, not a pixel check. The report explicitly says it is a queue-wide sample audit, not continuous playback, not a full fact-check, and not approval to publish.

props.heading: The limits in the output itself
props.body: Twelve frames per film at 70% position: catches settled-state defects, misses mid-animation states. Pantry flags come from metadata — shot.pantry_path et al — not from pixel inspection. The report quotes its own limits verbatim in the scope statement and the artifacts section.
props.quote: "This is a queue-wide source and sampled-visual audit, not continuous playback, a full fact-check, or approval to publish."
props.verdictLabel: The report knows what it is not.

beats.narration_text: write_review_queue_report.py is small and intentional. Two inputs, one output, no mutation. The three-spelling pantry check is backward compatibility named in the code. The no-try-except policy means failures are diagnostic, not silent. The report quotes its own limitations. Run it at the end of the audit pipeline and AUDIT.md is your deliverable — but it tells you exactly what it is not.

props.artifactHeading: The report writer, not the auditor
artifactLines: Two inputs in, one output out: audit.json + review-notes.json → AUDIT.md. The docstring makes read-only the top design contract — never mutate reels.
Three pantry spellings (pantry_path / pantry_file / pantry) reflect real schema evolution; backward compatibility is named in a comment, not hidden in a migration.
No try-except: crash-on-bad-input is the contract. Every error names exactly what is missing, so the failure is the diagnosis.

beats.narration_text: Here's the prompt. Paste this into Claude with your own reel batch in mind. Run audit_review_queue.py first to get audit.json and review-notes.json, then point write_review_queue_report.py at that output directory. Read the AUDIT.md it produces. Look at the pantry flags — are there beats waiting on human images? Check the master probe lines. Then ask: what would you change about the report structure itself? This is Liam, in for Bear.
